replies.author: Kindly_Life_947
replies.body:
**Why the full job is expensive**

Warhammer III runs on Creative Assembly’s in-house Warscape engine. You don’t get source code, only a stripped x86-64 binary. Ghidra or IDA turns it into pseudo-C with no function names, no variable names, no types or comments, and templates and inlining flattened into one blob.

* **Volume.** Original source runs about 10 tokens per line, so 1M lines is roughly 10M tokens. Decompiled output of the same logic is usually 2–4× longer and much less dense in meaning. A single read-through of everything is plausibly 30–50M tokens.
* **Agent overhead.** Agents don’t read code once. Each step resends context, rereads callers and callees, and revises guesses about what `FUN_14a3c2f0` does. Total tokens processed typically ends up 10–50× the raw size of the code. That puts a real attempt somewhere from hundreds of millions to a few billion tokens. Caching cuts the price but not the amount of work.
* **No global view.** No context window holds the whole engine, so you work one function or subsystem at a time. Recovering an architecture you have no names for is where the reasoning cost grows fastest.
* **Verification costs more than reading.** A fluent but wrong explanation of a decompiled function is cheap to produce. Confirming it means running the game, setting breakpoints and diffing memory. That loop, not the token bill, is the actual bottleneck.

replies.author: Affectionate_Fact854
replies.body:
You know even large games 100g plus , the game mechanics code is only like 5% of that 

Over 60% of it is textures, video snippets, sounds, meshes, localization (fonts)  and shader code 

Most of the other code is just the engine that runs the game and some devs also leaves unit tests for debugging code in there

Only a small portion is actual game mechanic code 

Just saying...

It's much more efficient and easy to reinvent the mechanic in different ways to make it work 

As there are never only 1 solution to a problem in code

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100
comments.body: Possibly. For more training data. But your logic is wrong. AI does not need to see something in training to recreate it. They definitely think. They can definitely create new things and solve new problems. If you understand combinations you know they produce massively large numbers very quickly. Like the number of ways you can order a deck of cards. Combinations give some of the largest numbers with actual meaning. There are just way too many prompts and way too many possible prompts. The AI hasn't been trained on all of that. Yet it can still provide responses.
